["Who boasts of lofty thoughts,
And braves on Augustus' throne,
The fortune of the dehumanized?
He who bore through all inevitability
Fire and water; borrowed storm and sword;
And did not despise feeling,
When now he was stuck in his most pressing need,
And saw no outcome but pale Death.

See, my insensitivity must praise
Those who greatly love seafaring,
Or rely on their rapier:
Who quickly caught the flame of a quick shaft of love
In their chest, through the lovely Blind maiden.
(That no water can extinguish,
Nor icy cold moisture appears so cool)
Without reason, despise my insensitivity.

Who then obtained in his legs
The rich man’s gout,
Or the gout, or the cheiragra,
Who then pain in his head; in his tooth;
And wished hellish fire instead of insensitivity?
Who was so cruelly distressed,
That he would rather suffer sorrow and evil;
Than through insensitivity seek benefit from his sorrow?

No Alcides, however mighty;
Bound by door and fire,
Never wished for awareness.
No Apollo who lost his charioteer,
By the power of Saturnides' flashing lightning,
And with tearful eyes,
And reason, my insensitivity was not loved;
And exalted above his divine being.

Let my insensitivity not sadden you,
Now you joyfully in this time,
Prince of honors, become another year older;
Although another, instead of your Tarte,
Would rather wish for Rodemont’s halberd.
Let us rather enjoy
Your generosity of tarts and fine wine,
Which from the knife and from pain will be insensitive.
Even Juppin, from his golden hall,
Offered his lightning bolt
For your father's buttocks.
No swift death was born of the plague,
By Apollo’s shaft.
Had Rome enjoyed that advantage,
Before Curtius bravely closed their pool!
Never a sorrowful end was their fate,
Never sorrowful, etc.

If, oh Prince, Love urged you
For a lively Maiden,
To firmly gird your dagger and saber to your body,
According to your inclination;
And that your hand, precisely in a fold,
Touched full of fish smell, yet is without smell;
Now that you have become another year older,
Now you again, etc.
The hot sun shone on his pale face,
Carthage had not corrupted him through the face:
Had Oedipus the blindness of Tiresias,
Had Oedipus the blindness of Tiresias
Enjoyed it,
His downfall was never heard of.

No jealousy of love comes to us through sight;
We do not see a woman go to bed with another.
The anger hence fled from Diana.
Had Cadmus after his vision yet lost in the cradle,
No one saw Actaeon’s crown.

Or although, oh Prince! our eye saw no light,
We see today your joyful birthday;
Faith shows us that the eye never understood:
Therefore we wish that you may separate blindly
From this world
As your years go down the drain.
In the tastelessness of the finest feeling.
Never does my brain remain tense
Before the court of reproachful jealousy:
But love with the splendor of men
Treats it rudely, with the roughest turmoil:

Delightful, still uncloaked, no child may truly call me;
I was never more insatiable:
Nothing can sadden me more,
Than to pour wine into my body;
And to stagger like a bear.
I hate wine with ice;
I despise the delicacy
In food, and drink, and smoke, and love, and beans.
Away with hares and rabbits,
With pastry, or tart or flan,
Away with French and Rhine wines:
Water can quench my thirst.

I spend no money on food or smoke, or unnecessary drinks.
I love neither nasturtium nor tobacco,
Nor other sharp odors.
I want to lightly thank you in the morning
For the ale or arrack,
I do not waste morning time
With greedy large breakfast
Of broths, or pâté de Mazarin:
At midday I banish from my table
All the fine beer and wine,
And I set the Struif and Waffle,
Beside the taste of Flemish cakes.
Life would please me lightly from Pythagoras,
If it were less Spartan,
I shall never lament Curtius,
Nor ask for other courage,
Than the use of knife and glass.
Away with Mark Antony,
His lust seems mockery to us;
Or though Cleopatra appeared so splendid,
I shall not lean after nectar drink,
Nor after other divinity:
Nor at the filthy Ptolemy
Shall all my taste and desire be spent.

Prince, who through art can give taste to tastelessness,
Let my song be tasteful to you:
So I desire, all my life,
To pursue no other taste;
Than Greek ambrosia.
Are you then having your birthday,
And create taste in tart,
Or a hare, or newly roasted chicken,
Let the taste of all else be abandoned
To hasten you to that dish,
Where the Blind and Deaf gather
To take off their hats for the taste.", 'Oh! What has happened to me,

['Hellish landlady  
Led me to wander at night  
To walk at midnight  
A stone turns under my foot  
A toe rolls in blood  
Stone inscriptions underfoot  
Blood-stained toes  
Hellish landlady  
Heard me coming home  
Was about to get out  
She started growling from the door  
Fighting from the back wall  
Pecking from the hearth edge:  
Look where a great eater comes from  
A great eater, a great drinker  
It eats even bull’s fodder  
It drinks beer from the barrel  
I hear, I answer:  
What does he eat for food?  
There is skin on top and bone beneath  
A little bit of lean meat in between  
What does he drink from the barrel of beer?  
There is foam on top and yeast beneath  
Sometimes a drop of good beer.', "I respect father  
I respect mother  
I respectfully pass to the brothers  
Yet the brothers are fighting  
The sisters-in-law nod  
That's where the big eater comes from  
Big eater, big drinker  
One who puts things in place  
The ox eats even his food  
The vat drinks even his drink  
I understand, I again respond  
What is there to eat from an ox  
The bone is below and the skin is above  
A stick of lean meat  
Or what to drink from that vat  
The yeast is below and the scum is above  
A drop of good beer.", "Master, little master!  
Mistress, little mistress!  
Said to eat a lot,  
Eat a lot, drink a lot.  
Put a lot in place.  
What will I eat at the village!  
What will I drink at the village!  
What will I put in place at the village!  
The ox eats even while eating,  
Drinks from the vat even while drinking.  
What can I eat from the ox!  
What can I drink from the ox!  
The skin is outside and the bone is inside.  
What can I drink from the vat!  
The yeast is below and the foam is above,  
A drop of red beer,  
I won't go, I won't rush,  
I leave this place.  
I pour to the other room.  
I give the place to others,  
Let the better ones come to the place,  
The more honest to the place,  
Let the most famous be at the door's side.  
I will come to see tomorrow,  
Then I will come back again.  
The order was where I left,  
The chair was where I raised,  
The bench was where I stayed.  
Sweep the room to the corner,  
Split kindling for the stove,  
The broom cried like a whisk.  
The clogs asked for cleaning,  
Spoons burned in the fire,  
The ladle handles got hot."]

Name: 2_village_inside_live_brooms
Representative_Docs:
['If it were my being,  
And secondly my doing,  
I would surely know what I would know:  
I would make the oxen into oxen,  
The horses into horses,  
The helpers into fathers,  
The boys into proud cranes,  
The girls into blossoms...  
I myself would be in the field,  
Plowing the furrow in the meadow,  
Letting the songs ring out,  
And the words be lovely to hear.  
Then the village would listen,  
The parish would watch closely,  
The forest would roar back,  
The grove would respond,  
Young women would smile,  
Men would ponder their thoughts,  
Children would quietly spy,  
Squatting by the village gate,  
Near the backyard of the household.  
Oh! If only it were my being,  
And secondly my doing;  
Surely I would know what I would know.', "If I were to exist  
Secondly, if I were to do  
I would surely know what I would do  
I would make the room face the wind  
Life upon a haystack  
A house upon a berry stalk  
A hut upon a dock leaf  
A boy comes to ask me  
Is there a town or a flag  
Or is there Keidela church  
Or is there a Finnish salt ship  
Or is there a Pärnu wreath ship  
But I understand, I answer:  
There is no town, nor is there a flag  
There is no Keidela church  
There is no Finnish salt ship  
Nor is there a Pärnu wreath ship  
This is my father's sauna  
Water has rolled the logs  
Fog has covered the doors  
Rain has mossed the walls  
A snowstorm had stuffed the room.", "If I were to exist  
If I were to act  
I would make the room face the wind  
The sauna face the big island  
Towards the cluster of rowan berries  
Under the broad oak's canopy  
So that the sun would not shine on us  
Nor the moon shine on us, either  
So I could call the sad girls  
And bring along the good fellows  
They would often make spinning wheels  
Bring spinning wheels inside  
Build bobbins too  
When our babies are tiny  
We will soon make spindles  
To hold the head celebrations  
To see the old women  
They are kind in the eyes of men  
Dear in the world of old bachelors."]
